USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture — keep the pending $200B List 3 (10%) tariffs as a credible, in-process threat, do not trigger them now, and keep the door open for a negotiated structural settlement on IP and technology transfer. Do not unilaterally roll back any of the already-imposed measures (that would forfeit leverage), but avoid pushing the $200B round through while China is signaling further retaliation and while farm-belt and business pressure is mounting. Signal willingness to talk if Beijing offers verifiable structural concessions, not just more purchase commitments.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to the US is real but sectorally concentrated and not yet systemic. The escalation is biting precisely where China can hurt the Trump base: USDA cut its US soybean export forecast ~11% (to 55.5m tonnes) and soybean prices are down ~20% since March, with Ohio/Illinois farm income projected down 30–63% (farm-policy sources, mid-July). That matches the 'key export sector exposed to retaliation, domestic political pressure mounting' band of the threat scale. Yet the broad economy is not impaired — the dollar is strong and rising (~113 broad index), the 10Y holds ~2.9%, consumer sentiment ~97.9 and industrial production are still firm, and CPI is low — so this is well below an existential reading and closer to a mild-to-moderate threat (≈+0.25). The US retains the initiative: it set the agenda (Section 301, tariffs, ZTE) and the $200B list gives continued negotiating leverage. However, the second-order risk argues against escalation now: triggering List 3 would spread tariffs onto consumer goods (TVs, clothing, bedding — LA Times, 7/10) and invite another round of Chinese retaliation on agriculture, with no clear exit path (CFR's Alden; Prasad warning the escalation removes the 'graceful retreat'). Escalating further would also amplify already-building domestic opposition from retailers and Senate Finance Chair Hatch ('reckless,' 'not a targeted approach'). The discipline is therefore to hold the escalation lever without pulling it, and to use the credible threat of List 3 and the WTO case to compel genuine structural change at the negotiating table rather than over-committing to a full-blown trade war that would harm US consumers and farmers alike.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold our current proportional retaliatory posture and pursue negotiation rather than escalating further. We should not be the party to initiate a new round of escalation; instead, use the active window (US List 3 is in public comment/hearing phase through late August, decision after Aug 31) to press for renewed talks, keep our WTO challenges alive, and signal willingness to bargain while making clear we will match any additional US escalation proportionally. Do not unilaterally concede, but do not invite the $200B tranche to be finalized.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high but not yet existential. US 25% tariffs on $34B of our goods are already in effect and List 2 (~$16B) is pending, with a proposed $200B additional 10% tranche published July 10 (event timeline 2018-07-10) that "will hit the Chinese export sector hard" (IHS Markit). Firm-level targeting is real: the April ZTE denial order has effectively shut ZTE down (event timeline 2018-04-16), and Trump has threatened duties on nearly all of China's annual US exports. Yet the macro shows we are not yet in crisis: June exports still rose 11.3% with a record $133.8bn H1 bilateral surplus, and the first-round tariff impact is estimated at only ~$5bn (Natixis) — which pushes me to +0.55 rather than toward the existential anchor. The reason I recommend negotiate rather than escalate is that our escalation capacity is structurally limited: after matching the $34B and a likely $16B list, only ~$80B of US imports remains for retaliation, so we cannot win a tit-for-tat tariff war (Mizuho). Escalating further would almost certainly help confirm Trump's $200B tranche and deepen damage to our export hubs, while a negotiated hold — backed by WTO challenges and a restrained posture — preserves our leverage and lets domestic reform/tech-autonomy efforts proceed. Hence threat +0.55, action +0.1 (negotiate), not escalate.
